content.title: About
content.content: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is a tuber crop cultivated worldwide. It is a major source of carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals. Potatoes are eaten boiled, baked, fried, and are used in mashed dishes, soups, and countless recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes were introduced to Europe from South America in the 16th century.
There are over 4,000 potato varieties differing in skin and flesh color.
Potato ranks fourth in global agricultural production after cereals, rice, and soy.
The Irish Potato Famine of the 1840s was caused by potato blight (Phytophthora infestans).
Potato tubers can store up to 20% of their dry weight as starch.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: A medium potato provides about 30% of the daily recommended vitamin C, supporting immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes contain more potassium than bananas, helping regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: The skin is high in fiber, which promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: Potatoes supply vitamins B6, B3, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: Green spots and sprouting eyes contain toxic solanine; these parts should be removed.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience a potato allergy.

items.title: Overeating may lead to weight gain
items.content: Because of their carbohydrate density, large portions can contribute to excess calorie intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Potatoes can be boiled, baked, fried, steamed, or mashed. Leaving the skin on (if clean) preserves fiber. For healthier meals, prefer baking or boiling with minimal added fat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store potatoes in a cool, dark, dry place, avoiding the refrigerator where they can become sweet. Keep them away from onions, as they accelerate each other's spoilage. Discard any tubers that are moldy, sprouted, or soft.
